migrationNotes: Spine: governments try to improve on what a market does. First by fixing a price, where a binding ceiling or floor leaves one side short, then by correcting a cost the market ignores, where a tax equal to the damage restores the efficient quantity.

lesson.title: Controls and spillovers

steps.headline: A ceiling below the market price

lead.text: Last lesson a tax changed a market from the outside. Another tool is to fix the price itself. A price ceiling is a legal maximum price, and a price floor is a legal minimum. Whether either one matters depends on where it sits compared with the price the market would reach by itself.

Go back to the lolly stall, where demand is Qd = 60 − 5P and supply is Qs = 5P, so the market settles at £6 and 30 lollies. The council sets a ceiling of £4. At that price buyers want 60 − 20 = 40 lollies, but sellers offer only 5 × 4 = 20. The ceiling is below the market price, so it binds: it holds the price down, and buyers want more than sellers will supply. The gap of 20 lollies is a shortage.

afterFigure.text: A sale needs a willing buyer and a willing seller, so only 20 lollies change hands, fewer than the 30 sold freely. The 20 buyers who miss out are left in a queue. Price no longer decides who gets a lolly, so something else has to, usually the order people arrive in or who they know.
A ceiling above £6, such as the £9 in the second case, would change nothing, because the market price is already below it. Only a control that stops the market reaching its own price has any effect.

lead.text: The council's £10 limit on tickets is a ceiling. Think about who decides how many tickets change hands at a capped price.

reveal.text: You compared the two quantities at the controlled price. Only 28 cups change hands, fewer than the 60 at equilibrium, so queues and connections ration the cups instead of price.

lead.text: In the coffee market a ceiling of £12 sits below the equilibrium price. Compare what buyers want with what sellers offer at £12.

steps.headline: A floor above the market price

lead.text: A price floor works from the other side. A floor above the market price binds, because it holds the price up. At the lolly stall a floor of £8 means buyers want 60 − 40 = 20 lollies, while sellers, tempted by the high price, offer 5 × 8 = 40. The 20 lollies in between are a surplus: goods on offer that nobody buys.

afterFigure.text: As with the ceiling, the smaller quantity decides how much is sold. Here buyers are the short side, so only 20 lollies change hands, again fewer than at the free price. Sellers who made the other 20 are left with stock.

A floor below £6, like the £4 in the second case, would change nothing, just as a ceiling above £6 did not. A control that binds always shrinks trade below what the free market would have done, and it leaves one side of the market wanting more than it can get.

Find the cups sellers offer at £26.

steps.headline: A cost nobody is billed for

lead.text: Prices can also go wrong in a quieter way. Take a fertiliser plant whose run-off pollutes a stream below it. Each tonne costs the plant money for materials and labour. Each tonne also does £2 of damage to the fishermen downstream, and the plant never sees that £2, because nobody sends it a bill. A cost borne by people outside the sale is called an external cost.

A market settles on the costs the firm actually pays and the values buyers actually place on the good. In the market with demand Qd = 60 − 5P and supply Qs = 5P, that means £6 and 30 tonnes. The 30th tonne is worth £6 to its buyer and costs the plant £6 to make, so the market sees no reason to stop there. But it also does £2 of damage, so it costs society £8.

afterFigure.text: So some of the 30 tonnes are worth less to buyers than they cost everyone together. The market counts only the cost the firm pays, so it makes more than is worth making. The next question checks that reading, and the screen after it counts the damage properly.

lead.text: Use the idea from the last screen on a paint firm: the damage to neighbours is in nobody's accounts.

To count the damage, add it to each tonne's cost. The firm's supply curve shows what each tonne costs the firm. What each tonne costs society is higher by the damage per tonne, so the social supply equation has P minus the damage wherever the firm's has P.
In the fertiliser market a £2 damage turns Qs = 5P into 5(P − 2) = 5P − 10. Setting that equal to demand gives 60 − 5P = 5P − 10, so 70 = 10P and P = 7. The quantity is 60 − 35 = 25 tonnes.

afterFigure.text: The efficient quantity is 25 tonnes, which is 5 fewer than the market makes. Each of those 5 tonnes is worth less to its buyer than it costs once the damage is added. The figure puts the plant's own cost curve beside the social one, and a larger damage lifts it further above and cuts the efficient quantity more. The algebra is the same as for a £2 tax in the last lesson, and that is no accident.

reveal.text: Counting the damage lifts the cost curve by £9. Social supply meets demand at £26 and 48 tonnes, 12 fewer than the market makes.

lead.text: Paint firms' own costs give Qs = 4P − 20, and each tonne does £9 of damage. Add the damage to supply, then meet demand.

Go back to the fertiliser plant, which makes 30 tonnes when 25 would be efficient. On each of the 5 extra tonnes, the cost to society exceeds the value to the buyer. For the 26th tonne the excess is small, and by the 30th tonne it has grown to the full £2 of damage. These losses form a triangle with base 5 and height 2, so the loss is ½ × 5 × 2 = £5. It is the deadweight loss of the unregulated market.

A tax that puts the damage on the firm's own bill removes it. Charge the plant £2 for each tonne, equal to the damage, and its costs now match society's, so it makes 25 tonnes. This is called a Pigouvian tax, after Arthur Pigou, the economist who proposed it in his 1920 book The Economics of Welfare.

afterFigure.text: Unlike the tax in the last lesson, this one does not lose surplus. The trades it stops are the ones that were not worth making once the damage was counted, so removing them leaves society better off.

reveal.text: On the 12 extra tonnes the gap between social cost and buyers' value grows from nothing at 48 to £9 at 60: a triangle of £54.

lead.text: In the paint market the damage is £9 a tonne. Measure what making too much costs.

lesson.orientation: Predict shortages and surpluses from price controls, and correct an external cost with a Pigouvian tax.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A city is hosting a sold-out concert, and tickets are changing hands at high prices. The council answers with a law: no ticket may be sold for more than £10. Fans cheer, since the price they were paying was much higher.

A price is a message as well as a bill. It tells buyers how much to take and sellers how much to offer, and a law that overrides it can leave the two sides wanting different amounts. Prices can also be wrong in a quieter way, when a firm's choices harm people outside the sale and nobody sends the firm the bill.

This lesson looks at both. We work out what a legal maximum and a legal minimum do to a market, then turn to a cost that falls on neighbours and see how a tax can put it back on the firm that causes it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict shortages and surpluses from price controls, and correct a cost that falls on other people.

recap.keyIdea: A control that binds stops buyers and sellers trading as they want: a ceiling creates a shortage, a floor a surplus. A cost that falls on others makes a market overproduce, and a tax equal to the damage corrects it.

blocks.text: Back at the concert, the £10 ceiling meant 300 tickets sold while more fans wanted one. In the coffee market you found a shortage of 48 cups under a £12 ceiling and 60 unsold under a £30 floor. The paint market overproduced by 12 tonnes, a loss of £54.

recap.nextHook: Throughout these lessons the costs of supply came as a given equation. The next lesson opens up a firm to see where its costs come from and how they decide how much it makes.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 4P − 20. A price ceiling of £12 is imposed. How large is the shortage, in cups?
hints: A ceiling below equilibrium is the price that actually applies.
Find quantity demanded and quantity supplied at the ceiling.
Subtract supply from demand.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At £12, Qd = 100 − 24 = 76 and Qs = 48 − 20 = 28, so the shortage is 76 − 28 = 48 cups.

questions.onCorrect: 48 cups. At the ceiling buyers want 76 and sellers offer 28: the gap is the shortage.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what buyers want. Subtract what sellers offer.
That is what sellers offer. The shortage is the gap between the two quantities.
That is the quantity at equilibrium. At the ceiling the two quantities differ.

hints: A floor above equilibrium holds the price at the floor.
Find both quantities at the floor.
Subtract demand from supply.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At £30, Qs = 120 − 20 = 100 and Qd = 100 − 60 = 40: 60 cups go unsold.

questions.onCorrect: 60 cups. At a floor above equilibrium sellers offer more than buyers take.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what sellers offer. Subtract what buyers take.

questions.prompt: A paint market has demand Qd = 100 − 2P and supply Qs = 4P − 20, where supply reflects firms' own costs. Each tonne also causes £9 of pollution damage to people nearby. What quantity, in tonnes, maximises total surplus once that damage is counted?
hints: Add the external cost to the firms' own cost of each tonne.
In the supply equation, that means replacing P by (P − 9).
Set that social supply equal to demand and solve for quantity.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Social supply is 4(P − 9) − 20. Setting it equal to 100 − 2P gives 156 = 6P, so P = £26 and Q = 100 − 52 = 48 tonnes.

questions.onCorrect: 48 tonnes. Add the damage to each tonne's cost, then meet demand.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the market quantity, which ignores the damage.
That is the price, not the quantity.

questions.prompt: In that paint market 60 tonnes are produced instead of the efficient 48, and each tonne does £9 of damage. What is the deadweight loss of the unregulated market, in pounds?
hints: The loss comes only from the overproduced tonnes.
On those tonnes the gap between social cost and value grows from zero to the external cost.
Take one half × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: £54. Over the overproduced tonnes the gap grows from nothing to the damage per tonne: a triangle.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the base only. Find the area.

questions.prompt: A price ceiling of £30 is set in a market whose equilibrium price is £20. What happens?
hints: Ask whether the legal maximum stops the market price being reached.

acceptedIdeas: The ceiling does not bind, and nothing changes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The market price of £20 is already below the £30 maximum, so the ceiling has no effect.

choices.label: The ceiling does not bind, and nothing changes

questions.onCorrect: Nothing changes. A ceiling above the equilibrium price never stops the market reaching it.

misconceptions.feedback: A shortage needs the ceiling to sit below the price the market would reach.
A surplus comes from a floor above equilibrium, not from a ceiling.

questions.prompt: A per-unit tax set equal to the marginal external cost of an activity is named after which economist? Surname only.
hints: He succeeded Alfred Marshall as professor of political economy at Cambridge.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pigou: Arthur Cecil Pigou, in The Economics of Welfare (1920).

questions.onCorrect: Pigou. A tax equal to the marginal external cost is called a Pigouvian tax.

questions.prompt: A paint market has demand Qd = 90 − 3P and supply Qs = 2P − 10, which reflects firms' own costs. Each tonne also causes £5 of damage to people nearby. What quantity, in tonnes, is efficient once the damage is counted?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Social supply is 2(P − 5) − 10 = 2P − 20. 90 − 3P = 2P − 20 gives P = £22, so Q = 90 − 66 = 24.
